title: Newton's Laws of Motion

standard_text: Newton's first law (inertia), second law (F = ma) and third law (action–reaction pairs); mass and weight; friction. (summary of the Intermediate Science curriculum, JSS 3, theme: You and Energy)
meta_desc: Free JSS 3 Intermediate Science worksheets (NERDC curriculum, theme: You and Energy): newton's laws of motion, resultant force and free-body diagrams, mass, weight and gravity, force, mass and acceleration and action and reaction. 100 questions with answers.
key_sub: Every action force has an equal and opposite reaction force on the other object.
body_html:
How to think about it

Newton's first law: an object stays at rest or moves at constant velocity unless a non-zero resultant force acts on it (inertia). Newton's second law: the resultant force equals mass × acceleration, Fnet = ma. Newton's third law: when An exerts a force on B, B exerts an equal and opposite force on A.

Weight w = mg (g = 9.8 m·s⁻²) acts downwards; the normal force acts perpendicular to the surface. Friction opposes motion: f = μN. On an incline of angle θ, the component of weight down the slope is mg sin θ and perpendicular to it is mg cos θ.

Example

A 1,200 kg car accelerates at 2 m·s⁻². Resultant force?

F = ma

Answer: 2,400 N

Example

Weight of a 50 kg student?

w = mg

Answer: 490 N

Common mistakes

  • Thinking a moving object always needs a resultant force.
  • Putting action–reaction forces on the same object.
  • Using mg as the normal force on a slope.

faq.q: Why do you lurch forward when a taxi brakes?
faq.a: Your body tends to keep moving forward (inertia) while the taxi slows down.

faq.q: Why does a seatbelt help in a crash?
faq.a: It provides the force that slows you down with the car, so you do not keep moving forward.

items.e: Acceleration depends on resultant force and mass.

items.q: How does a rocket move forward?

items.q: Funke writes an action force: “A cannon fires a cannonball forward.” What is the reaction force?
